title: Stunning Footage Captures China's Tiangong Space Station Transiting the Moon
summary: It's a challenge that requires split-second timing and a bit of luck: capturing a space station as it crosses the face of the Moon. On May 29, astrophotographer Efrain Morales pulled it off spectacularly, recording China's Tiangong space station in stunning detail as its silhouette buzzed Tycho Crater. Using a 12-inch telescope and an astronomy camera, Morales filmed the transit from Puerto Rico at 11:33 p.m. EDT. The entire event lasted less than a second. 'It is a challenge in less then a second to capture this event,' Morales told Space.com. 'Using a program the ISS Transit Finder helps in giving information to capture the space station. Adjusting the FOV and at times calculating last minute deviations in time and positions in which makes it more challenging.' In the footage, the orbital outpost appears to dive directly toward Tycho Crater, whose 53-mile-wide (85 kilometer) impact site and bright ejecta dominate the southern lunar region. The station's vast solar panels and habitable modules are sharply outlined against the Moon's surface. Also visible are the dark expanses of Mare Nubium (the Sea of Clouds) and Mare Nectaris (the Sea of Nectar)—ancient basaltic plains formed by lava flows billions of years ago. Tiangong, which translates to 'Heavenly Palace,' consists of the core module Tianhe and two laboratory modules, Mengtian and Wentian. It orbits Earth at an altitude between 217 and 280 miles (340 to 450 km). The station is currently crewed by three taikonauts from the Shenzhou 23 mission: commander Zhu Yangzhu, pilot Zhang Zhiyuan, and payload specialist Lai Ka-ying, who launched aboard a Long March 2F rocket on May 24. For those inspired to try their own hand at astrophotography, Morales's work shows what's possible with careful planning and the right equipment. Guides are available for tracking and photographing Tiangong, and with the station regularly passing overhead, patient skywatchers might just capture their own breathtaking transit—a fleeting reminder of humanity's growing presence in low Earth orbit.
why_it_matters: This event shows how space is no longer the domain of just governments; with accessible tools, anyone can witness and document orbital activities, blurring the line between professional and amateur astronomy and raising awareness of international cooperation and competition in space.

background_read: China’s Tiangong space station is the country’s first permanent outpost in orbit, with a core module launched in 2021 and two additional lab modules added by 2022. It is smaller than the International Space Station but marks a significant milestone in China’s independent space program, which has also sent robotic rovers to the Moon and Mars.

Astrophotography that captures a space station crossing the Moon or Sun is especially challenging because these transits last only a fraction of a second. Photographers must calculate the exact path — using tools like ISS Transit Finder — and set up equipment with extreme precision, sometimes adjusting for last-minute deviations in the station’s orbit. Tiangong orbits Earth at about 400 km altitude, similar to the ISS, and appears as a bright moving dot to the naked eye when it passes overhead.

The lunar features in the footage highlight a rich volcanic history. Tycho Crater, about 108 million years old, is one of the most prominent features on the Moon’s southern hemisphere, with a ray system of bright ejecta that stretches hundreds of kilometers. The dark ‘seas’ (mares) are vast plains of basaltic lava that erupted billions of years ago when the Moon was geologically active.

perspectives.description: Efrain Morales's work demonstrates that hobbyists with modest equipment can produce images that inspire the public and even contribute positional data for satellite tracking. It highlights how the democratization of technology allows everyday people to engage directly with space exploration.

While the transit is beautiful, some observers raise concerns about the growing number of objects in low Earth orbit—both functional stations and debris. Capturing images like this also reminds us of the need to manage orbital traffic to avoid collisions that could threaten all satellites.

Astrophotography sits at the intersection of technical skill and artistic composition. Choosing the exact moment when a silhouette crosses Tycho Crater is as much an aesthetic decision as a scientific one, showing that the human drive to explore space is partly about creating meaning and beauty.

perspectives.perspective: A future of increased LEO activity
perspectives.description: As more nations and companies launch stations and satellites, such transits will become more common. Forward-thinking planners imagine a time when 'space traffic reports' are as routine as weather forecasts, and these student and amateur captures become valuable for public engagement and even regulatory oversight.
